summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
According to the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 13.7% of firms in the nonprofit-heavy "Other services" category reported using AI in the prior two weeks, up from 12.6% in the prior period. This represents measured adoption within the sector, though the base remains modest. The Census methodology focuses on active two-week usage, which captures operational deployment rather than experimentation or pilot projects.

The nonprofit sector's AI adoption remains constrained by structural inequities and uneven access to technology resources. NTEN emphasizes that nonprofit technology adoption is marked by inequities within organizations and across the sector that must be addressed if nonprofits want to meet their communities' needs. The AI Equity Project operates with explicit focus on making artificial intelligence accessible and practical for underrepresented communities, operating learning pathways and support models to ensure underrepresented populations participate directly in deploying machine learning tools. This suggests that while some nonprofits deploy AI, access and capability gaps significantly limit adoption breadth.

The nonprofit ecosystem around AI remains sparse and narrowly specialized. Only four individually verified nonprofit and open-source organizations directly stewarding AI tooling and infrastructure are catalogued, and none function as compute or infrastructure builders. LMSYS operates Chatbot Arena for neutral model benchmarking, while Khan Academy uses AI capabilities in education delivery rather than producing them. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software tools with intersecting AI concerns, but their primary missions predate and are not defined by AI. This small roster indicates that AI infrastructure and governance within the nonprofit sector remain underdeveloped.

Funding and strategic capacity to deploy AI vary sharply across the sector. Candid tracks comprehensive grants and nonprofit data, noting that research on Black-led and women-of-color-led nonprofits reveals funding disparities and unequal access to support systems for long-term resources. The Center for Effective Philanthropy examines how nonprofits fare under historic challenges and how foundations respond, positioning AI adoption as part of broader operational effectiveness concerns. These organizations document the funding landscape rather than prescribing AI investment levels, indicating that nonprofits considering AI deployment must navigate both capability constraints and uneven access to capital for technology adoption.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid offers a comprehensive database of grants and nonprofit information that helps users locate funding and research organizations. Analysts, advocates, and philanthropists rely on the platform for a holistic view of social-sector activity. New research shows that women of color-led nonprofits receive funding for current work but have less access to support systems and flexible long-term resources. For our August LinkedIn Live conversation, we marked Black Philanthropy Month with a discussion about funding for Black-led nonprofits. We asked nonprofits whether they use third-party giving platforms to raise money, and Candid’s new interactive data visualization feature shows who funds what and where, who receives those grants, which populations are served, and trends over time. Join our email list to receive the latest insights, trends, product updates, and research from Candid.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.
